sections.skill: Estimate fuel, maintenance, and depreciation, and find the monthly cost of owning a car

questions.domain: Buying, Financing, and Owning a Vehicle
questions.prompt: Maya drives 12,000 miles a year in a car that gets 30 miles per gallon. Gas costs $3.50 a gallon. What is her yearly fuel cost?
questions.intro: Fuel cost = (miles ÷ miles per gallon) × price per gallon. First find the gallons used, then multiply by the price.
questions.topic: The cost of owning a car

misconceptions.A: Gives the gallons, not the dollars

sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.domain: Buying, Financing, and Owning a Vehicle
questions.prompt: A car bought for $30,000 loses 15% of its value each year. What is it worth after 2 years?
questions.intro: Depreciation is the loss in a car's value. A common model takes the same percent each year: value = price × (1 − rate)^years.
questions.topic: The cost of owning a car

misconceptions.B: Subtracts 15% of the original price each year

sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.domain: Buying, Financing, and Owning a Vehicle
questions.prompt: Maya's monthly costs: loan payment $386.66, insurance $150, fuel $117, maintenance $60. What is her monthly cost of owning the car?
questions.intro: The true cost of a car is much more than the loan payment. Add every regular cost: payment, insurance, fuel, maintenance, parking, and tolls.
questions.topic: The cost of owning a car
sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.domain: Buying, Financing, and Owning a Vehicle
questions.prompt: Car A gets 40 mpg and Car B gets 20 mpg. Each drives 10,000 miles a year with gas at $3.60. How much more does Car B spend on fuel each year?
questions.intro: Fuel cost = miles ÷ mpg × price. Compare the two totals.

questions.domain: Buying, Financing, and Owning a Vehicle
questions.prompt: What usually happens when an owner skips scheduled maintenance such as oil changes?

choices.text: Costlier repairs later
The car runs better because parts are not disturbed
Insurance pays for repairs caused by neglect
The warranty covers it no matter what

questions.intro: The owner's manual lists a maintenance schedule. Small regular costs (oil, filters, tires, brakes) prevent large repair bills.
questions.feedback: Skipped maintenance often leads to bigger, more expensive repairs.
questions.topic: The cost of owning a car

misconceptions.C: Insurance usually excludes wear and neglect

sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.domain: Buying, Financing, and Owning a Vehicle
questions.prompt: Which car cost stays the same each month no matter how much you drive?

choices.text: Gasoline, which depends on miles driven
Tolls, paid on each trip
An insurance premium
Tire wear, which grows with miles

questions.intro: Fixed costs (insurance, loan payment, registration) do not change with miles. Variable costs (fuel, tolls, wear) rise as you drive more.
questions.feedback: A premium is a fixed cost.
questions.topic: The cost of owning a car
sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.domain: Buying, Financing, and Owning a Vehicle
questions.prompt: What is depreciation?

choices.text: The interest charged on a car loan
A tax paid when a car is registered
The rise in a car's price because of inflation
The drop in a car's value over time

questions.correct_answer: The drop in a car's value over time
questions.feedback: Depreciation is the loss of value as a car ages.

sections.relationship: Depreciation is often modeled as a constant percent decrease each year.

questions.domain: Buying, Financing, and Owning a Vehicle
questions.prompt: Under a 15%-per-year model, how does the dollar drop in year 2 compare with year 1?

choices.text: It is larger, because cars lose value faster as they age
It is smaller
It is the same, because the rate is the same every year
It is zero, because cars stop losing value after one year

questions.intro: The same percent of a smaller value is a smaller dollar amount. Year 1: $4,500 lost. Year 2: $3,825 lost.
questions.feedback: 15% of a smaller value is fewer dollars.
questions.topic: The cost of owning a car
sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.prompt: Why can a 2- or 3-year-old car be a good value?

choices.text: Older cars never need any repairs at all
Used cars are exempt from sales tax everywhere
The steepest value loss has already happened
Insurance costs nothing on cars over two years old

questions.correct_answer: The steepest value loss has already happened
questions.feedback: A buyer of a lightly used car avoids the largest early depreciation.

questions.domain: Buying, Financing, and Owning a Vehicle
questions.prompt: A steady (not flashing) "check engine" light comes on, and the car is running normally with no warning signs such as smoke, overheating, or strange noises. What is the best first step?

choices.text: Have the code read soon
Ignore it until the car stops running completely
Disconnect the light so it stops bothering you
Sell the car right away at any price

questions.intro: Many auto parts stores and mechanics can read the warning code, which points to the problem. A flashing light or serious symptoms usually means stop driving and get help right away.
questions.feedback: Checking the code early can catch a problem before it gets worse and more expensive.
